newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade's EU perks seen mostly as political boost.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade's EU perks seen mostly as political boost.

text.p: The European Union's decision to grant trade privileges to Belgrade has more political than economic importance for a cash-strapped economy still encircled by an outer wall of sanctions, analysts said on Tuesday.
"It is a carrot, albeit a small one, but still a carrot in Europe's carrot-and-stick policy towards Belgrade. And it is very important as a political gesture," one Western diplomat told Reuters.

EU granted trade privileges to Yugoslavia last week but said the deal was for 1997 only and conditional on further democratic reforms and Belgrade's implementation of its commitments to the Dayton peace accord.
Government officials reacted with enthusiasm saying the restoration of trade preferentials was expected to result in a speedy resumption of bilateral cooperation between Yugoslavia and the EU.

"It is a step forward. The door (to EU) has been...opened for Yugoslavia to return to its pre-war position. It is a signal that Yugoslavia will be recognised one day," said a government source who asked not to be named.
Analysts were more cautious and said the move indicated that the EU had relaxed its pressure on Belgrade for further democratisation but clearly preserved its firm stand on the need for changes.
"Political pragmatism prevailed when they took the decision. They fear another Albania happening here," said Ljubivoje Acimovic of the Institute for International Politics and Economy.

The EU said the trade benefits -- which include offering duty-free access and eliminating quantitative restrictions on industrial products -- were also needed to help the country's struggling economy.
But analysts question how much the country would benefit from the move given the poor state of its economy and cast doubt that it would have any major financial effect.

"Economic effects will be minor. It takes much more for a crippled and outdated economy like ours to return to world markets and meet required standards," Zoran Popov of the Belgrade-based Economics Institute said.
The Institute for Market Research (IZIT) said trade preferentials could bring Yugoslavia no more than $100 million a year.
"Direct effects are difficult to estimate, but it will be a positive signal to other countries to renew cooperation with Yugoslavia," IZIT economist Snezana Popovcic-Avric said.
But Popov warned that Yugoslavia could offer only a very small number of products at competitive prices. "Quality is yet another issue," he said.
Analysts agreed EU trade benefits would help to some extent only sectors like agriculture, textile, footwear, food- and wood-processing industries.

"Capabilities of our economy are very limited and problems are huge. There is no money to finance export oriented production, improve quality, upgrade technology, cut production costs. The economy is simply not competitive enough," said IZIT chief economist Slobodan Milosavljevic.
Four years of war, sanctions, mismanagement and political upheaval have devastated the country's economy, emptied state coffers and pushed most of the country's population below the poverty line.
Foreign capital is seen as the only way to resuscitate the economy, which according to some estimates needs around two billion dollars annually by the year 2000 to avoid collapse.
Although the EU granted trade benefits to Yugoslavia, the country still has almost one billion dollars frozen on its bank accounts abroad due to sanctions.

The United Nations slapped a trade embargo on Belgrade in 1992 for its role in the Bosnian war. It was lifted last October, but a so-called "outer wall" was left in place while Serbia's behaviour was monitored, particularly in the mostly ethnic-Albanian province of Kosovo.
Yugoslavia's senior government officials promised even more and faster reforms after the EU move, but analysts insisted reforms could not be performed without sufficient funds.
"Reforms cost and we need money to finance them," the government source said. -- Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 222 4254
